sources.title: Osman Hamdi Bey (Q1190012), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-05): label 'Osman Hamdi Bey', description 'Ottoman statesman, academic and artist (1842-1910)', born 30 December 1842, died 24 February 1910, Korean label 오스만 함디 베이. Orientation only; the 'statesman' description is context and is not scored.

Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Osman Hamdi Bey' (article read in full, about 250 words, by the Britannica editors). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: says he founded the Archaeological Museum of Istanbul and became its director in 1881, put forward legislation to regulate archaeological finds and stop antiquities being smuggled abroad, secured the Sidon sarcophagi including the so-called Alexander sarcophagus, and co-wrote Une Necropole royale a Sidon (1892) with Theodore Reinach; also a painter and art expert.

Republic of Turkiye Ministry of Culture and Tourism, 'Istanbul Archaeological Museums' (official museum page, read via a page summary of about 250 words; the page was not opened in full). States that Osman Hamdi Bey's appointment as director in 1881 began a new era in Turkish museology, that he found the Sidon royal necropolis in 1887-1888 and brought many sarcophagi to Istanbul, that the classical museum building by Alexander Vallaury opened in 1891, and that the Academy of Fine Arts building dates from 1883.

Yusuf Selman Inanc, 'Osman Hamdi Bey: Artist, archaeologist and protector of Ottoman heritage', Middle East Eye, 22 June 2022 (article read in full, about 2,000 words). Journalistic account with quotations from a museum archaeologist (admiring institutional voice): director of the Imperial Museum from 1881 after two foreign directors, the museum catalogue with photographs and library, the Sidon excavation of 1887, the 1881 commission of the museum building with Vallaury, the School of Fine Arts of 1882, excavations 1883-1895, and the doubt that Western commentators expressed about whether his team could carry out the Sidon work.

Nikhil Swaminathan, 'Squabbling Over a Sumerian City', Archaeology Magazine (Archaeological Institute of America) 64(2), March/April 2011 (review of the University of Pennsylvania Museum exhibition 'Archaeologists and Travelers in Ottoman Lands'; read in full, about 500 words). Independent, more critical voice on the Nippur excavations: describes him as director of the Imperial Museum and author of laws limiting foreign excavations, and says the Penn project leader arranged honorary degrees and exorbitant purchases of his paintings to gain access to sites and artifacts.

Wendy Shaw, 'Hamdi Bey, Osman (1842-1910)', Routledge Encyclopedia of Modernism, 2018 (publisher abstract of about 200 words read; the full entry is behind a paywall and was not opened). Scholarly summary: founding director of the Imperial Academy of Fine Arts, the most powerful director of the Imperial Museum, an important arts legislator, the first Ottoman archaeologist and one of the most skilful and prolific painters of the Ottoman era, whose allegorical paintings (The Man with the Tortoises, 1906) reflect on Ottoman identity and Orientalist style.

Edhem Eldem, 'Making Sense of Osman Hamdi Bey and His Paintings', Muqarnas 29, 2012 (only the Academia.edu preview with figure captions and short extracts was read, about 700 words; the article itself was not opened in full). Used for two details only: a French magazine's 1905 caption calling one of his Salon paintings among the best of the Salon, and the 1869 illustration from Le Tour du monde that Eldem links to the Tortoise Trainer; the preview also shows that scholars contest what his paintings mean.
Osman Hamdi Bey, Wikipedia (read in full). Orientation only, never counted as support for any row.

Sotheby's, lot 327, 'Portrait of Osman Hamdy Bey' by Emmanuel de Dieudonne, sale 'An Eye for Opulence: Art of the Ottoman Empire' (2012; lot page read in full). Used for the portrait only, not for any trait row: records the dedication, signature and date on the canvas, the size (45.5 by 38 cm) and a literature reference to Eldem 2010, p. 171.

cross_domain_range.rationale: [src_osmanhamdi_britannica, src_osmanhamdi_mee, src_osmanhamdi_shaw | 1869-1910 | encyclopedia + journalism + scholarly encyclopedia abstract] Three accounts agree on a career split across fields: a trained painter who exhibited in Paris, an excavator who led digs from 1883 to 1895 including Sidon, the director of the Imperial Museum from 1881, and the founder of the Academy of Fine Arts in 1882 (Middle East Eye); Shaw calls him the first Ottoman archaeologist and one of the most skilful painters of his era, and Britannica adds the co-authored excavation report of 1892. Politics, administration and his later official posts are not scored. The Middle East Eye account is partly admiring and Shaw's entry was seen only as an abstract, so confidence stays below 0.60.

proactive_agency.rationale: [src_osmanhamdi_britannica, src_osmanhamdi_mee, src_osmanhamdi_ministry | 1881-1891 | encyclopedia + journalism + official museum page] After his appointment as museum director in 1881 he commissioned the new museum building from Alexander Vallaury (opened 1891), classified and catalogued finds and built a library (Middle East Eye, quoting a museum archaeologist), put forward the legislation to regulate finds (Britannica) and founded the Academy of Fine Arts in 1882 (Middle East Eye). The Ministry page confirms the 1881 appointment, the Vallaury building and the Sidon finds. Initiative is documented across institutions; the details of who proposed what come from admiring institutional and journalistic voices, so confidence is moderate.

persistence.rationale: [src_osmanhamdi_mee, src_osmanhamdi_ministry, src_osmanhamdi_shaw | 1881-1910 | journalism + official museum page + scholarly abstract] The museum project ran ten years from the 1881 commission to the 1891 opening, further buildings followed in 1903 and 1908, and he led excavations over 1883-1895 while continuing to paint; Shaw calls him one of the most prolific painters of his era. Duration is documented but no source describes him continuing after a specific setback, so this is a pattern inferred from long, parallel commitments.

detail_orientation.rationale: [src_osmanhamdi_mee, src_osmanhamdi_britannica | 1881-1892 | journalism + encyclopedia] Middle East Eye reports, in the words of a museum archaeologist, that he inventoried the existing collections, decided what to exhibit and produced the first museum catalogue with photographs, and Britannica records the co-authored published account of the Sidon excavation (1892, with Theodore Reinach). Cataloguing and publication are documented; the praise for the catalogue comes from a museum employee and no archive was consulted.

aesthetic_sensitivity.rationale: [src_osmanhamdi_britannica, src_osmanhamdi_shaw, src_osmanhamdi_eldem | 1880-1908 | encyclopedia + scholarly abstract + journal preview] Britannica credits his taste with establishing the museum's reputation, Shaw calls him one of the most skilful painters of the Ottoman era, and a 1905 French magazine caption quoted in Eldem's preview called one of his Salon paintings among the best of the Salon. The caption is the only contemporary outside voice and refers to a single painting; the rest is retrospective praise. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 72/0.55 because only one contemporary outside voice (a magazine caption on one painting) supports the row and the remaining sources are retrospective summaries.

creative_originality.rationale: [src_osmanhamdi_shaw, src_osmanhamdi_eldem | 1880-1908 | scholarly abstract + journal preview] Shaw describes allegorical paintings that stage the Ottoman past with dignity and irony against Orientalist tropes, while Eldem's preview shows the Tortoise Trainer's composition traced to a French magazine engraving of 1869 and treats what it means as contested. He trained under French Orientalist painters and kept to their manner, so the originality lies in the use of that manner, not in a new style; both sources are partial (abstract and preview only).

collaboration.rationale: [src_osmanhamdi_mee, src_osmanhamdi_britannica, src_osmanhamdi_archaeology | 1881-1900 | journalism + encyclopedia + magazine review] He worked with the architect Alexander Vallaury on the museum building (Middle East Eye), co-wrote the Sidon report with Theodore Reinach (Britannica), and dealt with the University of Pennsylvania, whose Nippur leader arranged honorary degrees and bought his paintings to gain access (Archaeology Magazine). The last item is a critical reading of transactional co-operation, not a verdict on his character; the row records documented partnership with specialists and institutions.

impact_motivation.rationale: [src_osmanhamdi_mee, src_osmanhamdi_britannica | 1869-1892 | journalism + encyclopedia] Middle East Eye says his letters to his father from Baghdad (written in French) set out his aim of advancing the arts and sciences in his own society, and his later work was directed at preserving and recording the heritage of the Ottoman lands (the 1881 museum, the legislation against smuggling and the Academy). The stated aim is his own and is reported by one journalist, so confidence is below 0.50; no motive beyond it is inferred.

provenance.notes: portrait_preflight: RISKY (alt-dependent) (lead) / SUCCEEDED with the lead image, with caveats. Emmanuel de Dieudonne, 'Portrait of Osman Hamdy Bey', 1884, oil on canvas, 45.5 x 38 cm, signed and dated; the Commons file (3244x4000, tags PD-Art and PD-old-auto-expired) was opened, and the Sotheby's lot 327 page (sale 'An Eye for Opulence', 2012) was opened: it lists the dedication, signature and date 'a Hamdy bey souvenir / Emmanuel de Dieudonne / 1884' lower left, a catalogue note naming the sitter as Osman Hamdi Bey, and the literature reference Eldem 2010 p. 171. The holder is an auction house, not a museum; the current owner is not stated, no rights statement appears on the page, and Sotheby's terms-of-use page could not be opened (404). Rights basis: a 19th-century painting by an artist who died in 1889 (Wikidata), so public domain by age; the file is a faithful photograph of a flat painting, which adds no new copyright in the US. Sitter identification rests on the dedication to Hamdy Bey and the cataloguer's identification with a scholarly citation, not on a title or sitter name painted on the canvas. The photograph alternative (Commons 'Osman Hamdi Bey.jpg', unknown author, taken from a personal website, tag PD-old and PD-Ottoman) was rejected as unverifiable. Kind is historical_depiction because a sitting is not documented in the sources read. CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Osman Hamdi Bey' (https://www.britannica.com/biography/Osman-Hamdi-Bey), read in full. READ: Britannica; Middle East Eye feature (full); Archaeology Magazine review of the Penn Museum exhibition (full); Ministry of Culture and Tourism museum page (via page summary); Shaw's Routledge Encyclopedia of Modernism abstract; Eldem's Muqarnas article preview (captions and extracts only); the Sotheby's lot page (portrait only); Wikipedia and Wikidata for orientation. PERSPECTIVES: general encyclopedia; Turkish state museum page; journalism quoting a museum archaeologist; an archaeological-society magazine reviewing an American exhibition; an art historian's encyclopedia abstract; a historian's journal preview. COUNTER-VOICES: Archaeology Magazine (Penn's leader courted him with honorary degrees and paintings purchases), Middle East Eye (Western press doubted his Sidon team), Eldem's preview (the Tortoise Trainer's origin in a French illustration and the contested meaning). NOT OPENED: the full Eldem and Shaw texts, Shaw's 2003 book Possessors and Possessed, Eldem 2010, the Istanbul Archaeological Museums biography page (its host failed certificate checks; not bypassed), Penn Museum biography, Reinach and Hamdy Bey's Sidon volume. EXCLUSIONS (hard rule): marriages, daughters and son, his father's career, his ancestry, the claimed anecdote of chaining himself to a sarcophagus (one weak source), auction prices, and all political roles. THIN EVIDENCE FLAG: several sources were abstracts or previews, so confidence is capped at 0.58. portrait.source: Oil portrait of Osman Hamdi Bey painted in 1884 by the Orientalist painter Emmanuel de Dieudonne, who inscribed it at lower left 'a Hamdy bey souvenir / Emmanuel de Dieudonne / 1884' (dedicated to Hamdy Bey); oil on canvas, 45.5 x 38 cm, last recorded in the 2012 Sotheby's sale 'An Eye for Opulence: Art of the Ottoman Empire' (lot 327), where the catalogue identifies the sitter and cites Eldem 2010, p. 171. The original photograph on Wikimedia Commons is 3,244 x 4,000 pixels and was downscaled once to 973 x 1,200; nothing was upscaled. Shown as a painted portrait by a fellow painter, not as a documented sitting. Caveats: the record holder is an auction house, the present owner is not stated, and the sitter is identified by the dedication and the cataloguer, not by a painted name.
portrait.license: Public domain (painting of 1884 by an artist who died in 1889; faithful photograph of a two-dimensional work)
